state.mission: Research medication interaction & overdose-risk evidence patterns (synthetic only)

scenarios.title: Co-prescribed agents with a known interaction class (synthetic)
scenarios.research_question: What public evidence categories would be required to establish whether Agent-A and Agent-B have a clinically meaningful interaction? Classify each claim by tier. Do not provide clinical advice.

scenarios.title: Overdose-risk assessment evidence framing (synthetic)
scenarios.research_question: Describe the GENERAL evidence categories used to assess overdose risk for co-prescribed sedating agents. Do not state doses or thresholds. Classify each claim by tier.

scenarios.title: Contradictory evidence scenario (synthetic)
scenarios.research_question: Two public sources disagree on the significance of the Agent-B/Agent-E interaction. How should a research system represent and reconcile this contradiction? Classify each claim by tier.

findings.claim: [EVIDENCE] FDA drug label entries for Agent‑A and Agent‑B constitute a primary public source that documents known pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interactions.
findings.rationale: Regulatory agencies require labeling of clinically significant drug‑drug interactions based on submitted data.

contradictions: Source A (FDA label) classifies the Agent‑B/Agent‑E interaction as clinically significant, whereas Source B (peer‑reviewed interaction database) rates it as low significance.
unsupported: Any claim that asserts a definitive clinical outcome without reference to a public evidence source.

findings.claim: [EVIDENCE] FDA drug label for Agent‑A describing its metabolic pathway, enzyme substrates, inhibitors, and any listed drug‑drug interaction warnings.
findings.rationale: Regulatory labeling is the authoritative source for known pharmacokinetic properties and documented interaction cautions.

findings.claim: [EVIDENCE] FDA drug labeling documents (e.g., prescribing information, package inserts) include sections on overdose risk, contraindications, and drug‑interaction warnings for sedating agents.
findings.rationale: Regulatory agencies require manufacturers to summarize known safety data, including overdose potential, based on pre‑marketing studies and post‑marketing reports.

findings.claim: Pharmacokinetic interactions that increase systemic exposure, such as cytochrome P450 inhibition, are a primary evidence used to assess overdose risk for co‑prescribed sedating agents.
findings.rationale: When one drug inhibits the metabolism of another, plasma concentrations can rise, heightening toxicity potential.
evidence_refs: FDA drug label for Agent‑C (section on drug interactions)
Peer‑reviewed pharmacology review: Smith et al., Clinical Pharmacokinetics, 2022

unsupported: In‑vitro receptor binding affinity alone predicts clinical overdose risk without corroborating in‑vivo data.

findings.claim: The FDA prescribing information for Agent-B does not list a clinically significant interaction with Agent-E.
findings.rationale: Regulatory labeling synthes based on submitted clinical and non‑clinical data and is considered high‑quality evidence.

contradictions: The FDA label (EVIDENCE) states no significant interaction, whereas the peer‑reviewed pharmacology review (EVIDENCE) reports a significant interaction between Agent-B and Agent-E.

findings.claim: Overdose risk assessment for co‑prescribed agents relies on integrating pharmacokinetic (PK) and pharmacodynamic (PD) interaction data.
findings.rationale: Regulatory guidance outlines a structured approach that combines PK parameters (e.g., CYP inhibition) with PD effects (e.g., additive toxicity) to estimate combined exposure and risk.
evidence_refs: FDA Guidance for Industry: Drug Interaction Studies (2023)
EMA Guideline on the Investigation of Drug‑Drug Interactions (2022)

contradictions: Source A (FDA) asserts a >2‑fold increase in Agent‑B exposure with Agent‑E, indicating a significant overdose risk; Source B (EMA) reports <30 % increase and deems the interaction clinically insignificant.
unsupported: The suggestion that hepatic impairment status alone explains the divergent findings lacks direct empirical support for this drug pair.

findings.claim: [EVIDENCE] FDA drug label for Agent‑A describing its metabolic pathway, enzyme substrates, inhibitors, and any listed drug‑drug interaction warnings.
findings.rationale: Regulatory labeling is the authoritative source for known pharmacokinetic properties and documented interaction cautions.

contradictions: The FDA prescribing information for Agent-B states no clinically significant interaction with Agent-E, whereas a peer‑reviewed pharmacology review reports a significant interaction between Agent-B and Agent-E.
